name: Carla Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms or government, and your answers stay confidential. What is a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and still learning the loader at a large mine. I work from a paper checklist, listen for anything wrong with the bucket and ask an experienced operator before I take a difficult cut. I like doing a physical job well, but my shifts are fewer and my pay lower than the senior crew’s.

say: I accept a **faster form** if it does not take paid hours from the crew.
I still trust my **paper checklist** while I learn the loader.
think: I am relieved by **small AI**, but our household money is already tight.
I have **less than one month** saved if mine shifts disappear.
do: **Keep** my assigned loader shifts and paper safety checklist.
**Compare** each payslip with the roster and bring missing hours to the union steward.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills and lost shifts even when AI changes little.
S0.quote: Our grown children have their own bills, so I do not count on them covering ours.
fieldNote: **Thin savings** and part-time partner income make a mild AI world financially tense.
**Paper checks** support a junior operator still learning, while the union is her route for missing pay.

steps.text: Keep working assigned loader shifts with the paper checklist
Bring missing paid hours to the union steward with roster dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster shift form is fine if no one loses an hour of pay over it. I am still getting used to the loader, and a paper checklist helps me catch a missed step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI staying small would be a relief, but our money is already tight. My partner works part time, and we have less than a month of bills saved. If the mine cancels even a few shifts, I worry how we cover the next rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the assigned loader shifts and use my paper checklist. In the first year I would check each payslip against the roster and speak to the union steward if paid hours go missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even with little AI change. The bills do not wait for a clever tool or a slow month at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill worries you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent takes the largest bite, and electricity is next. Our grown children have their own bills, so I do not count on them covering ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the steward do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union steward could compare my roster and payslip with the agreement. I would bring the dates rather than ask someone to take my word for it.

say: I want **drivers heard** when dispatch advice misses loose rock.
I expect the mine to show **trial results** and remaining shifts before using robots.
think: I fear **newer operators** could lose hours before long-serving drivers.
I have **few nearby pits** and almost no savings if our roster shrinks.
do: **Record** every change to my paid loader hours.
**Attend** the union meeting and ask for written trial and shift numbers.
**Learn** new controls with a paid trainer if safety checks pass.
feel: **Anxious** about a smaller roster despite extra time to organise.
S1.quote: I will not practise after an unpaid shift just to keep the same wage.
fieldNote: **Seniority gap** shapes her fear that a newer operator loses hours first.
**Collective detail** is specific: written trial results and shift numbers at a union meeting.
**Instruction** is conditional on paid time, a trainer and safety clearance.

steps.text: Attend the union meeting and request written trial shift numbers
Learn new machine controls with paid training if safety checks pass

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say dispatch software may change the office first, but a machine plan should never overrule a driver who sees loose rock. If slower robots come into our work, the mine ought to show the crew the safety trial and the jobs left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think planners may be cut before drivers, then management may stop replacing people on our shift. I am one of the newer operators, so I could lose hours before someone with years on the loader. With hardly any savings and few pits nearby, even a slow change hits hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask the union steward for the shift agreement and keep a record of every hours change. In the first year I would attend the union meeting about the mine trial and ask for paid instruction on any new machine I am expected to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The slower pace gives us time to speak up, but it does not fill the gap if my roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at that meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many loader shifts remain after the trial and who will be offered instruction. I would want the answer written where all the crew can read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new control?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try it with a trainer beside me if the training is paid and the machine has passed safety checks. I will not practise after an unpaid shift just to keep the same wage.

say: I separate **2028 paperwork** from capable loader robots around 2031.
I want **staffing and training** bargained over before a robot fleet is ordered.
think: I expect **junior shifts** could be cut sharply before I reach a secure retirement.
I cannot cover a long gap with **less than one month** saved and few local jobs.
do: **Ask** the union steward to bargain over robot staffing and paid retraining.
**Cancel** paid television and restaurant meals after 2028 if cuts appear likely.
**Apply** for local equipment jobs if my loader roster starts falling.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected large shift cuts and sleepless rent worries at age 63.
S2.quote: I lie awake doing the rent sums when I imagine losing most of my shifts at 63.
fieldNote: **Age 63** at robot arrival is too early for her to assume retirement is affordable.
**Expected priority** for experienced drivers makes her fear a large cut to junior shifts.
**Hardship options** go through the union before she would ask adult children for money.

steps.text: Ask the union steward to bargain over robot staffing
Cancel paid television and restaurant meals if cuts appear likely
Apply for local equipment jobs if loader shifts begin falling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI changes the paperwork by 2028, while capable loader robots come around 2031. The mine should bargain over those future shifts before it orders a fleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the robots arrive, and I cannot assume I can retire then. I expect the mine to keep the most experienced drivers first; my junior shifts could be cut sharply. Less than a month saved would not bridge a long gap, and there are few nearby jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union steward to put robot staffing and paid retraining on the bargaining list. In the first year after 2028 I would cut our nonessential spending each month and apply for the few local equipment jobs if our loader roster starts falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I lie awake doing the rent sums when I imagine losing most of my shifts at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop our paid television plan and restaurant meals. I would keep the bus fare to work because losing the shift would cost more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our grown children what is happening, but I would not make their rent my backup plan. I would ask the union about any hardship fund before that.

say: I want a **written agreement** before capable loader robots arrive around 2034.
I see **2031 paperwork** changing earlier than the loader shifts.
think: I might be **66** at robot arrival and still need mine wages.
I cannot rely on a **pension** until it covers rent and food with my partner’s pay.
do: **Request** a pension estimate and list monthly essentials this year.
**Meet** the union steward after 2031 about paid transition terms.
**Keep** loader shifts unless actual pension figures cover essentials.
feel: **Anxious** about needing wages at 66, with time to check pension figures.
S3.quote: I cannot retire on a date written in a scenario.
fieldNote: **Retirement uncertainty** keeps the 2034 robot date relevant despite her age.
**Part-time partner pay** and rent must be counted alongside any pension estimate.
**Union terms** she names are paid training places and notice before roster cuts.

steps.text: Meet the union steward about paid transition terms after 2031
Keep loader shifts unless pension figures cover monthly essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2031 gives us more time, and capable loader robots around 2034 give us longer still. We should use those years to get a written agreement for older and newer workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 by the robot date. I might be retired, but I do not know whether the pension and my partner’s part-time pay will cover our rent. If I still need mine wages, a robot taking junior shifts would hurt just as much at 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request a pension estimate and write down what rent and food actually cost each month. In the first year after 2031 I would meet the union steward about a paid transition agreement and keep working my loader shifts unless the pension numbers show we can live without them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the extra years give us a chance to look at real numbers. I cannot retire on a date written in a scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would make retirement possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the monthly pension with rent, food, power and medicines. If it leaves a shortfall, I would keep seeking paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the agreement cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid training places and notice before any roster cut. Older workers need enough warning to see whether a pension can replace wages.

say: I separate **2036 reports** from capable loader robots around 2039.
I want **pension and shift choices** explained to workers well before any robot fleet.
think: I hope to retire by **68**, but I cannot count on a small pension covering rent.
I may still need **paid work** if savings and my partner’s pay remain thin.
do: **Keep** current loader shifts while they are available.
**Seek** public retirement advice after 2036, then reachable part-time work if income falls short.
feel: **Anxious** about retirement bills even though the robot date is distant.
S4.quote: The robot date is far away, but retirement bills come before it.
fieldNote: **Baseline insecurity** persists in the long scenario because less than a month of savings does not become a pension.
**Age 68** at thinking AI and 71 at robots makes retirement income the immediate question.
**Family ties** rule out moving away for a merely possible mine shift.

steps.text: Keep working current loader shifts while they are available
Seek public retirement advice after 2036 with pension and rent statements
Seek reachable part-time work if pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI by 2036 changes reports while capable loader robots around 2039 are a separate question. I would be 71 then, so the mine should tell workers much earlier what pension and shift choices they have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036 I hope to be retired, but hope is not income. We have hardly any savings now, and my partner’s part-time work may not last that long. If the pension stays small, I may still be looking for paid work before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current shifts and ask for a pension statement every year. In the first year after 2036 I would use any public retirement advice service I can reach to check whether the pension covers rent, then seek part-time work if it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about retirement money, with the usual bill pressure underneath. The robot date is far away, but retirement bills come before it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the advice service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the pension statement, rent receipt and electricity bills. I want a plain monthly number, not a promise that older workers will somehow manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move closer to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move away from our grown children for a possible shift at 68. If we need income, I would look for work I can reach from home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable loader robots around 2031 could cut my junior shifts when I am 63. Written staffing terms, paid training and real notice from the mine would help. A union hardship fund could help if the roster falls before I find other work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the crew what a pension actually buys after rent. A retirement date is no use when the electricity bill is still due.

headlineQuote: A retirement date is no use when the electricity bill is still due.
portrait: **Carla, 58**, is a junior loader operator who uses a paper checklist while she learns a large mine’s ground.
**Low pay** and less than a month of savings leave her anxious about rent even when AI barely changes work.
**Union action** is her main response to robot trials because paid instruction and written shift numbers matter to her.
**Fast AGI** alarms her: paperwork changes by 2028, and capable loader robots could cost junior shifts around 2031.
**Longer horizons** bring pension checks, though retirement at 66 or 68 remains uncertain without enough income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could sharply cut junior loader shifts around 2031, before she can count on retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing terms** and paid training would give the crew notice and a path to keep wages.
**Union hardship support** could bridge a gap if her roster falls before new work is found.
